notes:
I couldn't find any real denominational split on Psalm 61. The pages I read disagree over two exegetical questions (questions about what the text means), not along church lines. Is the "end of the earth" in v. 2 a real exile or a picture of spiritual distance? And who is "the king" in vv. 6–7: David, his royal line, or the Messiah? I've labelled each teacher's tradition so you can see that opinions on both questions cut across traditions.

**Gaps (left out, as you asked):**
- **NET Bible notes:** the netbible.org page loaded the wrong text, so I have none.
- **Traditions:** nothing specifically Lutheran, Pentecostal, Anglican or Orthodox.
- **Popular modern teaching:** no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material.
- **Spurgeon's full Treasury of David page:** it loaded only site menus, so I've used just the excerpts the search showed.

---

**Whole psalm: setting and use**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says we don't know what situation prompted the psalm, but it seems to come after David became king. https://enduringword.com/media/psalm-61-hope-and-help-when-my-heart-is-overwhelmed/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the early church sang this psalm daily at Matins (morning prayer). It calls the later part, about the king, "somewhat obscure." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-61.html
- Maclaren (Expositor's Bible) sees the singer as an exile longing for the sanctuary, as in Psalm 63. He lays the psalm out as an opening verse, two pairs of "prayer + past mercy" verses (2–3, 4–5), a pair about the king (6–7), and a closing verse of praise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
- The Expositor's Dictionary of Texts guesses that David wrote it after Absalom's defeat but before returning to Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/edt/psalms/61.htm
- Utley (bible.org) calls it a royal psalm: how God treats the king shows how he treats the nation. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21560

---

**v. 1 — "Hear my cry… attend to my prayer"**
- Guzik: David asks God to answer, not just to hear. God hears all prayer in one sense, but not every prayer gets a favourable response, so David doesn't take one for granted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
- Pulpit: the Hebrew word *rinnah* means a shrill, piercing cry, which can express joy or grief. "Attend" means "hear and answer it." https://biblehub.com/psalms/61-1.htm
- Maclaren: the word usually describes shouts of joy. Here it shows how intense the plea is; it describes the sound, not the feeling behind it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
- Calvin (Reformed): "cry" shows strong inner feeling, whether spoken aloud or quietly. The doubled request teaches us to keep praying even when God hasn't visibly answered yet. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
- Gill (Baptist): he cites Aben Ezra's view that the first phrase means spoken, public prayer and the second means silent prayer of the heart. God hears both. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-1.html
- Augustine (Catholic/patristic): the title "unto the end" points to Christ. The voice in the psalm is that of Christ's whole body, the Church spread across the world, speaking as one man. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm

**v. 2 — "From the ends of the earth… Lead me to the rock that is higher than I"**
- **What "ends of the earth" means:**
  - Guzik: as far as we know, David never travelled far from the land. He was at the end of his own strength and understanding. Guzik quotes VanGemeren that the phrase can be a picture of despair and spiritual distance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
  - Maclaren: the psalmist measures distance "not as a map maker, but as a worshipper." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
  - Pulpit: the phrase would fit best on the lips of an exile in Assyria or Babylon. https://biblehub.com/psalms/61-2.htm
  - Utley: the rest of the psalm doesn't support a real exile, so it is a picture of feeling cut off. He reports that the Anchor Bible, using Ugaritic parallels, reads it as the grave (*Sheol*), meaning the psalmist faced death. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21560
- **"Faint" / "overwhelmed":** the literal sense is "covered," as if wrapped in gloom (Maclaren). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives "covered over with darkness." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-2.html
- **The rock:**
  - Ellicott: literally "upon the rock lead me," meaning a rock too high to climb alone; God must take him there and set him on it. He notes that some read it instead as a difficulty only God can help him overcome. https://biblehub.com/psalms/61-2.htm
  - Maclaren rejects the "rock of difficulty" reading as against how the Psalms use the word. Because there is no definite article, he won't call "rock" a title of God here, but he says the psalmist knew his only safety was God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
  - Guzik draws out three needs: stability, something above himself, and God to lead him there. He quotes Boice that David had hidden among the rocks of the Judean wilderness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
  - Calvin: the rock means safe protection that David can't reach unless God's hand lifts him. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_2/psalm_61_1-4.htm
- **Reading the rock as Christ (common in older Protestant teaching):**
  - Matthew Henry: God's power and promise are the rock, "This rock is Christ," and only God's power can bring us onto it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-2.html
  - An excerpt in Spurgeon's Treasury of David: a rock higher than a mighty king must be divine, which sets forth the deity of Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps061.cfm
  - Barnes: a Saviour on our own level couldn't help us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-2.htm
  - Guzik quotes F. B. Meyer that Christ is the rock higher than us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
- **Catholic/patristic:**
  - Augustine says only Christ's inheritance cries "from the ends of the earth": the nations promised to the Son in Psalm 2, that is, the Church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm
  - He also calls Christ both the Rock on which the Church is built and the tower in v. 3. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm

**v. 3 — "You have been my refuge, a tower of strength"**
- Guzik: present trust rests on past faithfulness; God himself had been David's shelter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
- Matthew Henry: because God has been a rock to him before, David trusts he will be again; God and his name are as strong as ever (Prov 18:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-2.htm
- Maclaren: "refuge" and "strong tower" parallel "rock." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
- Augustine: flee to the Tower by calling Christ to mind; the devil's darts can't follow you there. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm

**v. 4 — "Let me dwell in Your tent forever… the shelter of Your wings. Selah"**
- **Tent:**
  - Guzik: "tabernacle" just means tent. It may picture God hosting and protecting a weary guest, and VanGemeren links it to God living among Israel in a tent in the wilderness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
  - Maclaren: the tent is the sanctuary, perhaps because the ark was still kept in a tent. God's guests have the right to food and protection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
- **Wings:**
  - Maclaren: the "wings" may allude to the cherubim (winged angelic figures over the ark), but the inner reality matters more than the symbols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
  - Calvin also allows a possible cherubim reference. He adds that David didn't think God was confined to the tent; the symbol lifted his faith. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
- **Has David already returned?**
  - Barnes reads the verse as David's confidence that he'll be restored to public worship. He thinks David may also have looked beyond to heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-61.html
  - Calvin, by contrast, thinks David is already back from exile and rejoicing, valuing worship above his throne. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
- **Heaven reading:**
  - Pulpit: an exile can't mean the literal tent, so this is a spiritual dwelling in heaven, which the tabernacle pictured. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/61.htm
  - Matthew Henry: the tabernacle was a type of heaven (Heb 9). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_061.cfm
- **Utley:** "forever" is plural for emphasis. He thinks it means a long, happy life of fellowship with God at the temple. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-61
- **Augustine:** "forever" means the Church will remain on earth until the end of the age. Being covered by God's wings is why we're safe amid temptation. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm

**v. 5 — "You have heard my vows… the inheritance of those who fear Your name"**
- **What the vows were:**
  - Gill: the Septuagint has "prayers," since people often made vows when praying in trouble. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/web/psalms/61-5.html
  - Calvin: "vows" stands for prayers. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
  - Clarke (Methodist): repeated resolves to be wholly God's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-61.html
  - Benson (Methodist): God keeps account of our vows, so we should keep them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-5.htm
- **What the inheritance is.** This is the verse where the teachers differ most:
  - *The land, plus the blessings that came with it:* Maclaren. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm Perowne, as quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-5.html Utley. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-61
  - *Living in God's land and worshipping at his tabernacle:* Wesley (Methodist). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-5.html
  - *Heaven:* Gill (Baptist) rejects the land and tabernacle readings in favour of the heavenly glory. He notes that the Septuagint, Vulgate and Aben Ezra read "an inheritance to them that fear thy name." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-5.html
  - *A lasting heritage of happiness for the godly:* Calvin (Reformed), unlike the brief prosperity of the wicked. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
  - *Length of days:* Ellicott, following the King James reading, citing Deut 17:19–20. https://biblehub.com/psalms/61-5.htm
  - *Rule over God's people:* Guzik. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
  - *God himself as the portion:* Matthew Henry. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_061.cfm
  - *The privileges of God's adopted children, including prayer:* Barnes. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/web/psalms/61-5.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the land had been threatened by Absalom's rebels and was now restored to those who fear God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-5.htm

**v. 6 — "Increase the days of the king's life… many generations"**
- **Who is the king?** This is the main interpretive debate, and it cuts across traditions:
  - *David himself:*
    - Barnes: David had expected death in Absalom's revolt. Barnes calls this more natural than an "ideal" king or a dynasty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-6.htm
    - Maclaren (Baptist): "he" and "I" are the same person, as v. 8 shows. Maclaren says no Messianic "diversion" is needed, though only Christ's kingdom fully fulfils the prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
    - Cambridge Bible: David speaks of himself in the third person as king, and the verse is a confident appeal to God's promise, not a request. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-6.htm
  - *David's royal line:* Hengstenberg, as reported in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-61.html
  - *The succession down to Christ:* Calvin (Reformed). https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
  - *Primarily the Messiah:*
    - Pulpit: "perhaps the best" reading. https://biblehub.com/psalms/61-6.htm
    - Gill (Baptist): "rather the King Messiah," who died, rose and lives forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-6.html
    - Geneva Study Bible: chiefly Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-6.htm
    - Coffman: the words "cannot possibly" refer to David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-6.html
  - *Both David and the Messiah:*
    - Matthew Henry: David himself, and the Messiah whom he foreshadowed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-6.html
    - Benson (Methodist): David, partly because his kingdom passed to his heirs, and partly because Christ would hold it forever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-6.htm
  - *Other proposals:*
    - Some suggest an exile praying for a later king, probably Josiah (reported in Pulpit). https://biblehub.com/psalms/61-6.htm
    - Clarke dates the psalm after the exile. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-5.html
- **Jewish evidence:** the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) reads "King Messiah." Keil & Delitzsch take this to show how the Jewish community read "king" after David's line ended. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-6.htm
- **Utley and VanGemeren:**
  - Utley calls the wording "royal hyperbole" (deliberate exaggeration). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21560
  - VanGemeren (quoted by Guzik) compares it to "God save the queen." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
- **Augustine:** Christ reigns now in his Church, and the saints will reign with him in days without end. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm

**v. 7 — "May he sit enthroned in God's presence forever; appoint Your loving devotion and Your faithfulness to guard him"**
- **"Abide" / "sit":**
  - Benson: literally "he shall sit," that is, on the throne, ruling in God's presence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-6.htm
  - Clarke (via Guzik): he will always appear before God for us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
  - Calvin: this repeats v. 4, meaning security under God's protection. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
  - Barnes: no more danger of exile, possibly with a hint of heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-61.html
- **Mercy and truth as guards:**
  - Maclaren: God's lovingkindness and faithfulness are pictured as armed sentries. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/61.htm
  - Utley: they are personified agents (compare Ps 23:6, 43:3), and upholding the king means upholding Israel. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21560
  - Calvin: the Hebrew verb can mean "appoint." He prefers the reading that God surrounds the king with his own mercy and faithfulness, rather than one that gives the king those virtues. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
  - Matthew Henry: David asks for God's mercy and truth, not a bodyguard or a fortress. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-6.html
- **Messianic reading:** Gill applies the verse to God preserving Christ's people and his spiritual kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/61-7.html
- **Augustine:**
  - Mercy is God forgiving sins without regard to merit; truth is his keeping his promises. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm
  - He then applies it morally: we should show mercy to the weak and to enemies, and live truthfully by not sinning. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801061.htm

**v. 8 — "Then I will ever sing praise… fulfill my vows day by day"**
- Guzik: the psalm moves from a fainting heart to daily, lifelong praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-61/
- Keil & Delitzsch: "so" means in response to these answered prayers. David will make his whole life one continuous paying of vows. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/61-6.htm
- Matthew Henry: praise is daily work because mercies are new each day. If we begrudge doing it daily, we can't expect to do it forever. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_061.cfm
- Calvin: the same David who prayed in trouble stayed grateful after deliverance. https://ccel.org/study/Psalm_61
- Utley: the vows were probably paid in the temple, perhaps with a thank offering. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21560
- Pulpit: the verse implies the writer goes on living and conscious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/61.htm
